questions.question_text:
The school wants to decide which new soup to offer at lunch.
Which survey question matches this purpose?

options.text: Which soup would you be most likely to buy: tomato, pumpkin, chicken, another soup, or none?
How many times did you buy lunch last week?
options.why: This counts past lunch purchases but does not identify a preferred soup.

options.text: Which dessert should the canteen sell?
options.why: This asks about desserts, so it does not address the soup decision.

options.text: Do you like eating at school?
options.why: This asks about school eating generally and gives no soup preference.

questions.solution_text: The matching question names the soup choice, offers the planned options, and allows other or none.

questions.question_text: A questionnaire asks, ‘How would you rate our fruit selection: excellent, good or satisfactory?’ What is the problem with the response choices?

options.text: There is no suitable response for someone who thinks the selection is poor.
The choices ask two separate questions.
options.why: This mistakes several response choices for a double question; the item asks only for a rating.

options.text: The choices include a negative rating.
options.why: This incorrectly treats satisfactory as a negative rating; none of the choices expresses a poor opinion.

options.text: There are too many choices for anyone to answer.
options.why: This mistakes the number of choices for the problem; the missing negative response is the fault.

questions.solution_text: All three choices are positive. Someone who thinks the fruit selection is poor has no suitable response.

questions.question_text:
The canteen wants to know students' usual weekly lunch purchases.
Which version makes the question ‘How many do you buy?’ clear and matches this purpose?

options.text: How many canteen lunches do you buy in a usual school week?
How many do you usually buy?
options.why: This still fails to name the item being counted.

options.text: Do you buy lots of lunches?
options.why: The word ‘lots’ has no fixed meaning and does not produce a precise count.

options.text: How many lunches have you ever bought?
options.why: The lifetime time period is impractical and does not match usual weekly buying.

questions.solution_text: The clear version names the item and fixes the time period as one usual school week.

questions.question_text: Which question is neutral when comparing two possible canteen snacks?

options.text: Would you prefer yoghurt, popcorn, or neither?
Surely healthy yoghurt is better than salty popcorn?
options.why: The approving and disapproving descriptions push students towards yoghurt.

options.text: Isn't popcorn the tastiest snack?
options.why: The word ‘tastiest’ and the question's wording suggest choosing popcorn.

options.text: Why should everyone choose yoghurt?
options.why: This assumes yoghurt should be chosen instead of asking for a preference.

questions.solution_text: The neutral item names both snacks without praise or criticism and includes neither.

questions.question_text: A lunch survey asks, ‘Which bread do you prefer: white or wholemeal?’ Which revision best covers students with other preferences?

options.text: White, wholemeal, another type, or I do not eat bread
White or wholemeal only
options.why: This repeats the missing-options problem and excludes other responses.

options.text: White, wholemeal, or both
options.why: This still excludes students who prefer another bread or no bread.

options.text: Every kind of bread sold in Australia
options.why: This creates an impractically long list instead of using an inclusive other option.

questions.solution_text: The complete set retains the main choices and includes both another type and no bread.

questions.question_text: A draft item asks, ‘Do you enjoy the canteen pasta and buy it every week?’ Which criticism explains why one yes or no may not give a clear answer?

options.text: A student may enjoy the pasta but not buy it every week, so the two parts can have different answers.
Both parts mention pasta, so they must have the same answer.
options.why: This assumes that enjoyment and weekly buying are the same thing because they concern the same food.

options.text: The question tells students that the pasta is delicious.
options.why: This invents leading praise that is absent from the question.

options.text: The question gives no time period for buying the pasta.
options.why: This overlooks the stated time period, ‘every week’.

questions.solution_text: The item asks about both enjoyment and weekly buying. A student can enjoy the pasta without buying it every week, so one yes or no cannot show both answers clearly.
